description: Artemis VI: Our project transforms NASA’s historical and scientific data into an interactive storytelling experience, bringing iconic rovers and landers back to life and revealing the journeys that paved humanity’s path to the stars.
summary:
We built an interactive 3D web atlas that lets users explore real, historical human-made hardware abandoned on the Moon and Mars — rovers, landers, descent stages, and surface instruments spanning 1966 to 2024. Rather than a static map, the app renders the Moon and Mars as true, rotatable 3D globes built from NASA-derived surface imagery, with glowing markers placed at verified landing coordinates for 30+ missions, including Apollo descent stages, Soviet Luna/Lunokhod landers, the Mars Exploration Rovers, Viking landers, Chang'e/Yutu rovers, Chandrayaan-3, and more.

Clicking any marker opens a full mission dossier: arrival date, status, coordinates (clearly labeled "confirmed" or "approximate"), the story behind the hardware, linked official sources, and mission video.

This directly addresses the challenge by turning scattered historical mission data into a single, explorable, emotionally engaging record of humanity's off-world footprint — making it easy to see, at a glance, everything we've left behind and why it mattered scientifically.

It matters because this hardware represents irreplaceable milestones in space exploration, yet its stories are fragmented across dozens of agency archives. By mapping it on real 3D terrain with verified coordinates, we help students, educators, and space enthusiasts appreciate the Moon and Mars not as empty worlds, but as sites of human history.
details:
What does it do / how does it work?

Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive 3D web application that maps real, historical human-made equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars — rovers, landers, descent stages, and surface instruments spanning missions from 1966 (Luna 9) to 2024 (SLIM, Odysseus). Users choose a world, then freely drag to orbit and zoom a true 3D globe (not a flat map) rendered from NASA-derived surface imagery. Glowing markers sit at each object's real landing coordinates; clicking one opens a quick-view card, and "Explore Full Story" opens a full dossier — mission name, arrival date, current status, coordinates (explicitly labeled "confirmed" or "approximate"), a narrative description, a linked official source, and a mission video. A search bar and filters (by equipment type and mission) let users narrow the 33 mapped objects across both worlds.

Benefits & intended impact

Mission histories for this equipment are scattered across dozens of agency archives (NASA, Roscosmos/Soviet Luna program, CNSA, ISRO, JAXA, ESA), making it hard for students, educators, or the public to see the full picture. By placing everything on one explorable, visually engaging 3D surface, the project turns fragmented historical data into an accessible, emotionally resonant learning tool — reframing the Moon and Mars not as empty rocks, but as sites of documented human history, each marker a real "I was here" left by a robot or a person.

Tools & technologies

- React + Vite (frontend framework/build tool)

- Three.js, via React Three Fiber and drei (the 3D rotatable globe, markers, starfield)

- Tailwind CSS (styling) and Framer Motion (animation/transitions)

- React Router (multi-page site: Home, About, Contact, Explorer)

- Data sources: NASA/JPL and NSSDC mission pages, Wikipedia mission archives, NASA-derived surface texture imagery (Clementine/USGS for the Moon, Viking MDIM for Mars)

- No hardware — a pure software/web submission

Creativity

Rather than a conventional dashboard or slideshow of facts, the project frames exploration itself as the interaction: you drive the discovery by orbiting a real planet and finding markers yourself, which mirrors the "digital space archaeology" framing of the project. The visual language (starfield, glassmorphism panels, gold/blue "mission control" accents) was designed to feel like a space-agency product rather than a generic web template.

Factors our team considered

- Scientific accuracy first: every coordinate is sourced, and we explicitly flag "confirmed" vs. "approximate" locations rather than presenting uncertain data as fact; we never invented a coordinate or mission detail.

- Graceful degradation: broken images or unavailable videos never crash the experience — they fall back to clear placeholders.

- Accessibility/performance: lightweight 3D rendering, lazy loading, and responsive layout for desktop and mobile.

- Attribution: every imagery and data source is credited on the About page.
